source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
description: Lucky bamboo is not a bamboo at all. It is a tropical, perennial shrub from West Africa and a member of the asparagus family (Asparagaceae). The species epithet commemorates German-born nurseryman and orchid specialist Henry Frederick Conrad Sander, of St. Albans, England. Lucky bamboo is a popular, easy-to-grow and undemanding houseplant outside of the tropical zone. It performs well in containers with partial shade outdoors in summer or bright but indirect light indoors all year. It requires a moist potting mix, or it can be grown in chlorine-free water. Change the water weekly (to prevent mosquitoes) and provide a weak liquid fertilizer. Putting some pebbles in the bottom gives a place for the roots to grow (and gives weight to the container to prevent it from tipping over). The bright green, strappy leaves are widely spaced along the upright stems, giving the plant an open, airy appearance. The stems are often trained into a variety of shapes (e.g., braided or spiral). Lucky bamboo rarely blooms as a houseplant. Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems: No serious insect pests or diseases. Monitor for mealybugs, mites and scale insects. Overwatering can cause yellowing of the leaves and rotting of the stems. Low humidity can cause browning of the leaf tips. More information on Dracaena .

Country Or Region Of Origin: West Central Tropical Africa to North East Angola
Light: Dappled Sunlight (Shade through upper canopy all day)
Deep shade (Less than 2 hours to no direct sunlight)
Flower Description: Small white flowers in clusters. Rarely blooms as a house plant.
Leaf Description: Bright green to gray-green strappy leaves are widely spaced along the upright stems
Stem Description: Thick green fleshy stem resembling bamboo.
Poison Symptoms: Toxic, if ingested, for cats and dogs. Vomiting (occasionally with blood), depression, anorexia, hypersalivation, dilated pupils (cats). Humans should not eat this plant. The sap can cause skin irritation.
